claim: Lin A/15 neuroblast generates 29 adult motoneurons per ganglion responsible for innervating leg muscles during the adult stage.
source: This lineage also produces most of the astrocytes and ensheathing glia of the thoracic ganglion (Baek and Mann, 2009; Brierley et al., 2012; Enriquez et al., 2018, Figure 1A–B4).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work and reference to Figure 1A-B4

claim: Lin A/15 neuroblast produces astrocytes and ensheathing glia of the thoracic ganglion.
source: This lineage also produces most of the astrocytes and ensheathing glia of the thoracic ganglion (Baek and Mann, 2009; Brierley et al., 2012; Enriquez et al., 2018, Figure 1A–B4).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work and reference to Figure 1

claim: Lin A/15 neuroblast follows a type Ib division pattern during larval stages.
source: The process of division in Lin A/15 NB during larval stages follows a particular pattern termed type Ib (Figure 1C–G).
evidence: Directly stated in text with reference to Figure 1C-G

claim: Lin A/15 neuroblast initially generates intermediate mother cells (IMCs) that give rise to a postmitotic cell and a proliferative glioblast.
source: Initially, Lin A/15 NB generates intermediate mother cells (IMCs) that give rise to a postmitotic cell and a proliferative glioblast (Figure 1G).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 1G

claim: Lin A/15 neuroblast switches to a classical type I division mode during a second phase, producing only postmitotic motoneurons.
source: Subsequently, during a second phase, Lin A/15 switches to a classical type I division mode, producing only postmitotic MNs (Figure 1G, Enriquez et al., 2018).
evidence: Directly stated with citation and figure reference

claim: Lin A/15 neuroblast produces an excess of neurons during larval stages that are selectively eliminated before reaching the adult stage.
source: Interestingly, during larval stages, Lin A/15 NB produces an excess of neurons, which are selectively eliminated before reaching the adult stage (Figure 1F).
evidence: Directly stated with reference to Figure 1F

claim: During the first phase of Lin A/15 division (40-49 hr after larval hatching), no apoptotic cells are observed.
source: During the first phase, 40–49 hr after larval hatching (ALH), no cDcp1+ cells were observed, confirming our previous study that during early developmental stages Lin A/15 NB produces an IMC that divides once to produce a glioblast and a postmitotic MN (Figure 2A1–A3, Enriquez et al., 2018).
evidence: Directly stated with citation and figure reference

claim: During the second phase of Lin A/15 division (53-96 hr after larval hatching), apoptotic cells that are cDcp1+ and Elav- are detected close to the neuroblast.
source: During the second phase, 53–96 hr ALH, apoptotic cells cDcp1+ Elav were detected close to Dpn+ Lin A/15 NB (Dpn and Elav are NB and postmitotic neuronal markers, respectively), suggesting that PCD occurs soon after asymmetric division.

claim: The sibling cells produced during the second phase of Lin A/15 division die before acquiring a neuronal identity.
source: The absence of Elav in the apoptotic cells also suggested that the sibling cells die before acquiring a neuronal identity (Figure 2B1–F3).
evidence: Inference from absence of Elav marker in apoptotic cells

claim: cDcp1+ Elav- cells do not express VGlut in late third instar larvae.
source: We dissected late third instar larva (LL3) and observed that cDcp1+ Elav cells did not express VGlut (Figure 2G1–G3).
evidence: Direct observation reported with figure reference

claim: Lin A/15 GMCs produce one motoneuron and a sibling cell eliminated by programmed cell death during the second phase of Lin A division.
source: Together, our results show that Lin A/15 GMCs produce an MN and a sibling cell eliminated by PCD during the second phase of Lin A division (Figure 2H).
evidence: Summary statement of results with figure reference

claim: Programmed cell death of the sibling cell occurs soon after birth before they express neuronal markers such as Elav or VGlut.
source: Moreover, PCD of the sibling cell occurs soon after birth before they express neuronal marker such as Elav or VGlut.

claim: Lin A/15 neuroblast continues proliferating from 0 hr after pupa formation until 20 hr after pupa formation.
source: We revealed that Lin A/15 NB (PH3+/Dpn+) continues proliferating from 0 hr after pupa formation (APF) until 20 hr APF (Figure 3A1–C3).

claim: During early pupal stages, cDcp1+ Elav- cells are detected, suggesting Lin A/15 neuroblast keeps producing a GMC that divides once into a motoneuron and an apoptotic cell.
source: During early pupal stages, cDcp1+Elav− cells were also detected, suggesting that Lin A/15 NB keeps producing a GMC that divides once into an MN and an apoptotic cell (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observation with inference and figure reference

claim: At 24 hr after pupa formation, Lin A/15 neuroblast is no longer detected in most samples (N = 4/17 samples with a neuroblast).
source: At 24 hr APF, Lin A/15 NB is no longer detected in most of our samples (N = 4/17, number of Lin A/15 with an NB), revealing the end of Lin A/15 neurogenesis at this stage.

claim: The volume of Lin A/15 neuroblast decreases throughout development until the termination of Lin A/15 neurogenesis.
source: Similar to what has been shown for other NBs, the volume of Lin A/15 NB decreases throughout development until the termination of Lin A/15 neurogenesis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Observation with comparison to other NBs and figure reference

claim: At 24 hr after pupa formation, the remaining Lin A/15 neuroblasts are extremely small and express cDcp1, suggesting decommissioning through programmed cell death.
source: At 24 hr APF, the remaining Lin A/15 NBs are extremely small and express cDcp1, suggesting a decommissioning of Lin A/15 NB through PCD (Figure 3D).
evidence: Observation with inference and figure reference

claim: Inhibiting programmed cell death in Lin A/15 by using P35 protein allows the neuroblast to survive at least until 28 hr after pupa formation.
source: To confirm this result, we then inhibited PCD in Lin A/15 by using the baculovirus P35 protein, an inhibitor of apoptosis in insects (Hay et al., 1994). Under these experimental conditions, Lin A/15 NB survived at least until 28 hr APF (Figure 3E–G).
evidence: Experimental manipulation with citation and figure reference

claim: Autophagic markers such as Atg8 and LysoTracker are not detected in the Lin A/15 neuroblast, suggesting that programmed cell death of the neuroblast is not linked to autophagy.
source: Furthermore, we did not detect autophagic markers in the NB, such as Atg8 and LysoTracker (Mauvezin et al., 2014) suggesting that the PCD of the NB is not linked to autophagy such as the mushroom body NBs (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Observation with citation and figure reference

claim: Lin A/15 neuroblast continues producing motoneurons during early pupal stages.
source: Our results reveal that Lin A/15 NB continues producing MNs during early pupal stages and, unlike most NBs described in the thoracic segments of the VNC (Maurange et al., 2008), Lin A/15 NB terminates its proliferative phase through PCD at 24 hr APF in all thoracic ganglia (Figure 3H).
evidence: Summary statement with citation and figure reference

claim: Lin A/15 neuroblast terminates its proliferative phase through programmed cell death at 24 hr after pupa formation in all thoracic ganglia.
source: Our results reveal that Lin A/15 NB continues producing MNs during early pupal stages and, unlike most NBs described in the thoracic segments of the VNC (Maurange et al., 2008), Lin A/15 NB terminates its proliferative phase through PCD at 24 hr APF in all thoracic ganglia (Figure 3H).
evidence: Summary statement with citation and figure reference

claim: At early L3 stages (46-49 hr after larval hatching), Imp protein and Imp RNA are highly expressed in Lin A/15 neuroblast, while Syp protein and Syp RNA are not detectable.
source: At early L3 stages (46–49 hr ALH), Imp protein and Imp RNA are highly expressed in Lin A/15 NB, while Syp protein and Syp RNA are not detectable (Figure 4A, F, G, L).

claim: At mid-L3 larval stages (70-73 hr after larval hatching), Lin A/15 neuroblast starts to express Syp protein and Syp RNA, and the expression of Imp begins to decrease.
source: As neurogenesis progresses to mid-L3 larval stages (70–73 hr ALH), Lin A/15 NB starts to express Syp protein and Syp RNA, and the expression of Imp begins to decrease (Figure 4B, F, H, L).

claim: Toward the end of larval stages, Imp protein and Imp RNA are weakly expressed in Lin A/15 neuroblast, while Syp protein and Syp RNA are highly expressed.
source: Toward the end of the larval stages, there is a reversal in the expression pattern: Imp protein and Imp RNA are weakly expressed, while Syp protein and Syp RNA are highly expressed (Figure 4C, F1, L).

claim: During pupal stages, Imp protein and Imp RNA are no longer detectable in the Lin A/15 neuroblast just before decommissioning.
source: This opposite expression pattern of Imp and Syp becomes more pronounced during pupal stages, where Imp protein and Imp RNA are no longer detectable in the NB just before decommissioning (Figure 4D–F, J–L).

claim: Knocking down Imp in Lin A/15 neuroblast results in premature decommissioning at 20 hr after pupa formation.
source: Knocking down Imp in Lin A/15 NB resulted in premature decommissioning at 20 hr APF (Figure 5A–G).

claim: Prolonging the expression of Imp leads to an extension of Lin A/15 neuroblast's lifespan until the young adult stages.
source: Conversely, prolonging the expression of Imp or knocking down Syp led to an extension of Lin A/15 NB's lifespan until the young adult stages and at least 28 hr after pupa formation (APF), respectively (Figure 5H–Q).

claim: Knocking down Syp leads to an extension of Lin A/15 neuroblast's lifespan to at least 28 hr after pupa formation.
source: Conversely, prolonging the expression of Imp or knocking down Syp led to an extension of Lin A/15 NB's lifespan until the young adult stages and at least 28 hr after pupa formation (APF), respectively (Figure 5H–Q).

claim: The temporal expression of Imp/Syp controls the timing of Lin A/15 neuroblast decommissioning similarly in all thoracic segments.
source: Furthermore, we observed that the temporal expression of Imp/Syp controls the timing of Lin A/15 NB decommissioning similarly in all thoracic segments.

claim: At 0 hr after pupa formation, Lin A/15 reaches its maximum number of Elav+ neurons (N = 39, SD = 2).
source: At 0 hr APF, Lin A/15 reaches its maximum number of Elav+ neurons (N = 39, SD = 2, number of Lin A/15 Elav+ neurons) (Figure 7K).

claim: The number of Elav+ neurons in Lin A/15 progressively decreases from 0 hr after pupa formation until reaching almost the final number of motoneurons at 24 hr after pupa formation (N = 32, SD = 1 at 24 hr APF compared to adult: N = 29, SD = 1).
source: However, even though Lin A/15 NB continues to divide in early pupal stages (Figure 3A–C), the number of Elav+ neurons progressively decreases until reaching almost the final number of MNs at 24 hr APF (N = 32, SD = 1 at 24 hr APF compared to adult: N = 29, SD = 1) (Figure 7K).

claim: Elav+ cDcp1+ neurons are detected close to the neuroblast during pupal stages, indicating that the last-born Elav+ neurons are progressively eliminated by apoptosis from 0 to 24 hr after pupa formation.
source: Unlike in larval stages, we detected Elav+ cDcp1+ neurons close to the NB, indicating that the last-born Elav+ neurons are progressively eliminated by apoptosis from 0 to 24 hr APF (Figure 6A1–C3).

claim: The first-born motoneurons are Edu- (N = 30, SD = 2) and located away from the neuroblast at 5 hr after pupa formation.
source: The first-born MNs were Edu− (N = 30, SD = 2, average number of Edu− MNs at 5 hr APF) and located away from the NB, while the last-born MNs (N = 7, SD = 2, number of Edu+ MNs at 5 hr APF) were Edu+ and positioned close to the NB (Figure 6D5–D7).
evidence: Direct quantification from EdU labeling experiment with figure reference

claim: The last-born motoneurons are Edu+ (N = 7, SD = 2) and positioned close to the neuroblast at 5 hr after pupa formation.
source: The first-born MNs were Edu− (N = 30, SD = 2, average number of Edu− MNs at 5 hr APF) and located away from the NB, while the last-born MNs (N = 7, SD = 2, number of Edu+ MNs at 5 hr APF) were Edu+ and positioned close to the NB (Figure 6D5–D7).
evidence: Direct quantification from EdU labeling experiment with figure reference

claim: cDcp1+ Elav+ neurons are always Edu+, and no cDcp1+ Edu- neurons are observed (N = 16 Lin A/15 analyzed).
source: Additionally, we found that cDcp1+ Elav+ neurons were always Edu+, and no cDcp1+ Edu− neurons were observed (N = 16, number of Lin A/15 analyzed).

claim: At 17 hr after pupa formation, there is a significant decrease in the number of Elav+ Edu+ motoneurons (N = 2, SD = 2), confirming the progressive elimination of all late-born motoneurons.
source: Further dissection of CNSs at late pupal stage (17 hr APF) showed a significant decrease in the number of Elav+ Edu+ MNs (N = 2, SD = 2, number of Edu+ MNs at 17 hr APF), confirming the progressive elimination of all these late-born MNs (Figure 6D1–F).

claim: Inhibiting apoptosis in motoneurons by ectopically expressing P35 results in similar numbers of neurons produced in L3 larvae compared to wild-type Lin A/15, while more Lin A motoneurons survive into adulthood.
source: As anticipated with this genetic manipulation, we observed similar numbers of neurons produced in L3 larvae in the Lin A/15 MARCM clone expressing P35 compared to the WT Lin A/15, while more Lin A MNs survived into adulthood (Figure 6F–J).

claim: Only the last-born neurons are precisely and progressively eliminated through programmed cell death during pupal stages from 0 to 24 hr after pupa formation.
source: Overall, our results provide strong evidence that the elimination of supernumerary MNs by PCD is not random. Instead, only the last-born neurons are precisely and progressively eliminated through PCD during pupal stages from 0 to 24 hr APF (Figure 6L).

claim: Imp is highly abundant in first-born motoneurons, while Syp is highly present in late-born motoneurons.
source: The serially derived neuronal progenies of the NB express Imp or Syp according to the expression levels in the NB: Imp is highly abundant in first-born MNs, while Syp is highly present in late-born MNs (Figure 4A–J).

claim: During larval stages, Imp and Syp are actively transcribed in postmitotic motoneurons.
source: While this could be the case here, our previous studies revealed that during larval stages, Imp and Syp are also actively transcribed in postmitotic MNs (Guan et al., 2022c).

claim: There is an opposite gradient of Imp and Syp expression according to birth order in late third instar larvae, with Imp expression progressively decreasing and Syp expression progressively increasing in older motoneurons.
source: Using this parameter to identify older versus younger MNs, we found an opposite gradient of Imp and Syp expression according to birth order, with Imp expression progressively decreasing and Syp expression progressively increasing in older MNs (Figure 7).

claim: During pupal stages, the last-born Lin A/15 motoneurons that are eliminated by programmed cell death are Imp- and Syp+.
source: Notably, during pupal stages, the last-born Lin A/15 MNs that are eliminated by PCD are Imp− and Syp+ (Figure 8A1–A5).

claim: Knocking down Imp in Lin A/15 results in premature programmed cell death of Elav+ motoneurons during larval stages.
source: Knocking down Imp in Lin A/15 resulted in premature PCD of Elav+ MNs during larval stages (Figure 8C1–D3) and an increase in the number of Elav+ neurons eliminated by PCD during pupal stages (Figure 8B1).

claim: Knocking down Imp in Lin A/15 results in an increase in the number of Elav+ neurons eliminated by programmed cell death during pupal stages.
source: Knocking down Imp in Lin A/15 resulted in premature PCD of Elav+ MNs during larval stages (Figure 8C1–D3) and an increase in the number of Elav+ neurons eliminated by PCD during pupal stages (Figure 8B1).

claim: Prolonging the expression of Imp or knocking down Syp in Lin A/15 neuroblast and its progeny inhibits programmed cell death of the supernumerary neurons.
source: Conversely, by prolonging the expression of Imp or knocking down Syp in Lin A/15 NB and its progeny, we were able to inhibit PCD of the supernumerary neurons (Figure 8B2, E1–J3).

claim: Manipulating the levels of Imp and Syp in the neuroblast and its postmitotic progeny leads to changes in the final number of neurons produced by Lin A/15.
source: These genetic experiments, which manipulated the levels of Imp and Syp in the NB and its postmitotic progeny, led to changes in the final number of neurons produced by Lin A/15 (Figure 8K) by altering the timing of NB decommissioning and the pattern of PCD in postmitotic neurons.
evidence: Summary of experimental results with figure reference

claim: Ectopically expressing Imp in postmitotic neurons results in more Lin A motoneurons being maintained in adult flies.
source: Under this experimental condition, more Lin A MNs were maintained in adult flies (Figure 8L1–N), implying a cell-autonomous function of Imp in promoting cell survival of MNs.

claim: Imp has a cell-autonomous function in promoting cell survival of motoneurons.
source: Under this experimental condition, more Lin A MNs were maintained in adult flies (Figure 8L1–N), implying a cell-autonomous function of Imp in promoting cell survival of MNs.
evidence: Inference from experimental results with figure reference

claim: Syp overexpression MARCM clones do not show a significant effect on the number of motoneurons produced in adult flies.
source: Additionally, we generated Syp overexpression MARCM clones, and interestingly, we did not observe any significant effect on the number of MNs produced in adult flies (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).

claim: The opposite expression pattern of Imp and probably Syp in postmitotic neurons precisely shapes the size of Lin A/15 lineage by controlling the pattern of programmed cell death in immature motoneurons.
source: In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that the opposite expression pattern of Imp and probably Syp in postmitotic neurons precisely shapes the size of Lin A/15 lineage by controlling the pattern of PCD in iMNs (Figure 8).

claim: Last-born motoneurons express a specific combination of transcription factors with high levels of Nvy and RunxA and no expression of Jim.
source: Our results revealed that last-born MNs express a specific combination of TFs, with high levels of Nvy and RunxA and no expression of Jim (Figure 9A, E1, M).

claim: Overexpressing Imp increases the number of Jim+ motoneurons from 8 to 15.
source: By overexpressing Imp or knocking down Syp in Lin A/15 NB and its progeny, the number of Jim+ MNs increased from 8 to 15 and 14 MNs, respectively (Figure 9A1–A3, B1–B3, C1–C3).
evidence: Experimental manipulation with quantification and figure reference

claim: Knocking down Syp increases the number of Jim+ motoneurons from 8 to 14.
source: By overexpressing Imp or knocking down Syp in Lin A/15 NB and its progeny, the number of Jim+ MNs increased from 8 to 15 and 14 MNs, respectively (Figure 9A1–A3, B1–B3, C1–C3).
evidence: Experimental manipulation with quantification and figure reference

claim: Last-born motoneurons express Jim de novo when Imp is overexpressed or Syp is knocked down.
source: Positive Cell Cluster Detection (PCCD) analysis demonstrated that last-born MNs express Jim de novo when Imp is overexpressed or Syp is knocked down (Figure 9A4, B4, C4, M).

claim: RunxA is expressed in two clusters of motoneurons in young and in last-born motoneurons with high level of expression in the motoneurons eliminated by programmed cell death during pupal stages.
source: RunxA is expressed in two cluster of MNs in young and in last-born MNs with high level of expression in the MNs eliminated by PCD during the pupal Stages (Figure 9E1–E4, M).

claim: Overexpression of Imp or knockdown of Syp drastically reduces the number of RunxA+ motoneurons.
source: The overexpression of Imp or the knowing down of Syp reduce drastically the number RunxA+ MNs (Figure 9F1–F3, G1–G3, H1–H2).

claim: The expression of RunxA is completely abolished in last-born motoneurons when Imp is overexpressed or Syp is knocked down.
source: The PCCD method reveals that the expression is completely abolished in last-born MNs while it is not affected in the youngest cluster of MNs when Imp is overexpressed or Syp knocked down (Figure 9F4, G4, M).

claim: Overexpression of Imp or knockdown of Syp slightly reduces the number of Nvy+ motoneurons from 16 to 11.
source: The overexpression of Imp or the knockdown of Syp slightly reduces the number of Nvy+ MNs from 16 to 11 MNs (Figure 9J1–L2).
evidence: Experimental manipulation with quantification and figure reference

claim: The number of motoneurons expressing Nvy is only reduced in the last-born cluster when Imp is overexpressed or Syp is knocked down, while it is not affected in the youngest cluster.
source: PCCD analysis shows that the number of MNs expressing Nvy is only reduced in the last-born cluster of MNs when Imp is overexpressed or Syp is knocked down, while it is not affected in the youngest cluster of MNs (Figure 9J4, K4, M).

claim: Overexpressing Imp or knocking down Syp changes the combination of transcription factors in last-born motoneurons from Nvyhigh, RunxAhigh, and Jim- to Nvylow, RunxA-, and Jim+.
source: Overall, these results demonstrate that overexpressing Imp or knocking down Syp changes the combination of TFs in last-born MNs from Nvyhigh, RunxAhigh, and Jim− to Nvylow, RunxA−, and Jim+.

claim: Overexpressing Jim in last-born motoneurons increases the number of motoneurons produced by Lin A/15 to approximately 32.
source: When we overexpressed Jim (Figure 10C1–C3), including in the last-born MNs, or removed Nvy (Figure 10B1–B3), the number of MNs produced by Lin A/15 increased to approximately 32 (Figure 10E).

claim: Removing Nvy increases the number of motoneurons produced by Lin A/15 to approximately 32.
source: When we overexpressed Jim (Figure 10C1–C3), including in the last-born MNs, or removed Nvy (Figure 10B1–B3), the number of MNs produced by Lin A/15 increased to approximately 32 (Figure 10E).

claim: In nvy-/- Lin A/15 MARCM clones overexpressing Jim, the number of motoneurons produced is close to 50.
source: Notably, in nvy−/− Lin A/15 MARCM clones overexpressing Jim (Figure 10D1–D3), the number of MNs produced is close to 50 (Figure 10E).
evidence: Experimental manipulation with quantification and figure reference

claim: Imposing a transcription factor code in last-born motoneurons resembling the code found in early-born motoneurons enables their survival until the adult stage.
source: These results demonstrate that imposing a TF code in last-born MNs resembling the code found in early-born MNs enables their survival until the adult stage.

claim: The specific combination of transcription factors controlled by Imp and Syp plays a crucial role in determining the fate and survival of motor neurons during development.
source: This suggests that the specific combination of TFs controlled by Imp and Syp plays a crucial role in determining the fate and survival of motor neurons during development.

claim: Two intrinsic temporal factors, Imp and Syp, actively participate in defining the final clonal size of a lineage by signaling the timely apoptosis of neuroblasts.
source: We found that two intrinsic temporal factors, Imp and Syp, actively participate in defining the final clonal size of a lineage by signaling the timely apoptosis of NBs.

claim: In some brain lineages, Imp and Syp cross-repress each other.
source: In some brain lineages, Imp and Syp cross-repress each other (Liu et al., 2015; Syed et al., 2017), and this cross-repression is influenced by external cues such as the ecdysone hormone (Homem et al., 2014) or activins (Rossi and Desplan, 2020).

claim: In Lin A/15 neuroblast, there is no mutual inhibition between Imp and Syp.
source: However, in Lin A/15 NB, we observed that there is no mutual inhibition between Imp and Syp, suggesting that Imp/Syp-independent mechanisms regulate their sequential expression in Lin A/15 NB (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).

claim: Imp and Syp are versatile proteins that play roles in various aspects of neuroblast development.
source: Imp and Syp are versatile proteins that play roles in various aspects of NB development.

claim: The opposite temporal expression of Imp and Syp in brain neuroblasts controls the temporal identity of the neuroblast.
source: Their opposite temporal expression in brain NBs controls the temporal identity of the NB (Liu et al., 2015; Syed et al., 2017), the timing of NB decommissioning (Yang et al., 2017), and the speed of cell division (Samuels et al., 2020).

claim: The opposite temporal expression of Imp and Syp in brain neuroblasts controls the timing of neuroblast decommissioning.
source: Their opposite temporal expression in brain NBs controls the temporal identity of the NB (Liu et al., 2015; Syed et al., 2017), the timing of NB decommissioning (Yang et al., 2017), and the speed of cell division (Samuels et al., 2020).

claim: The opposite temporal expression of Imp and Syp in brain neuroblasts controls the speed of cell division.
source: Their opposite temporal expression in brain NBs controls the temporal identity of the NB (Liu et al., 2015; Syed et al., 2017), the timing of NB decommissioning (Yang et al., 2017), and the speed of cell division (Samuels et al., 2020).

claim: In the brain, the opposing temporal expression of Imp and Syp in mushroom body neuroblasts shapes the expression pattern of the Chinmo transcription factor.
source: In the brain, their opposing temporal expression in mushroom body NBs shapes the expression pattern of the Chinmo TF, which, in turn, determines the identity of the neuronal progeny based on its concentration.

claim: Imp and Syp regulate the expression of terminal selector genes.
source: Additionally, Imp and Syp appear to regulate the expression of terminal selector genes.

claim: In the mushroom body, Imp and Syp shape the terminal molecular features by regulating the terminal selector Mamo.
source: In the mushroom body, Imp and Syp shape the terminal molecular features by regulating the terminal selector Mamo (Liu et al., 2019).

claim: Imp and Syp control the morphology of Lin A/15 motoneurons by determining the temporal identity of the neuroblast.
source: We have recently revealed that Imp and Syp not only control the morphology of Lin A/15 MNs by determining the temporal identity of the NB but also by shaping a combination of mTFs in postmitotic MNs, which subsequently control their morphologies (Guan et al., 2022c).

claim: Imp and Syp control the morphology of Lin A/15 motoneurons by shaping a combination of morphological transcription factors in postmitotic motoneurons.
source: We have recently revealed that Imp and Syp not only control the morphology of Lin A/15 MNs by determining the temporal identity of the NB but also by shaping a combination of mTFs in postmitotic MNs, which subsequently control their morphologies (Guan et al., 2022c).

claim: Motoneurons eliminated by programmed cell death during metamorphosis express a different combination of transcription factors compared to surviving motoneurons.
source: Here, we show that MNs eliminated by PCD during metamorphosis express a different combination of TFs compared to surviving MNs.

claim: Changing the opposite expression of Imp and Syp in Lin A/15 alters the transcription factor code not only in the surviving motoneurons but also in the motoneurons eliminated by apoptosis.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that changing the opposite expression of Imp and Syp in Lin A/15 alters the TF code not only in the surviving MNs but also in the MNs eliminated by apoptosis.

claim: The regulation of programmed cell death in immature motoneurons by Imp and Syp is dependent on transcription factors.
source: These MNs adopt a TF code similar to that of MNs that survive, suggesting that the regulation of PCD in iMNs by Imp and Syp is dependent on TFs.

claim: Both Imp and Syp control two parameters in postmitotic neurons: neuronal diversity and neuronal survival.
source: Taken together, all these data highlight that both RBPs control two parameters in postmitotic neurons: neuronal diversity and neuronal survival.

claim: Neuronal diversity and neuronal survival are directly coordinated through the regulation of transcription factors by Imp and Syp.
source: These two parameters are directly coordinated through the regulation of TFs by Imp and Syp.

claim: Programmed cell death is observed in various animal models from C. elegans to vertebrates.
source: PCD is observed in various animal models studied in laboratories, from C. elegans to vertebrates, and several explanations have been proposed to understand why such mechanisms have been selected during evolution (Dekkers et al., 2013; Oppenheim, 1991).

claim: Neurons normally fated to die may represent an important reservoir that can be used during evolution to explore different morphological possibilities.
source: The widespread occurrence of PCD during neurodevelopment leads to an intriguing hypothesis that neurons normally fated to die represent an important reservoir that can be used during evolution to explore different morphological possibilities.

claim: Imp and Syp are evolutionarily conserved.
source: Imp and Syp are evolutionarily conserved, both homologs are highly expressed in the developing mouse brain and play vital roles in neural development, suggesting a fundamental conservation of their function in the development of central nervous (Chen et al., 2012; Mori et al., 2001; Williams et al., 2016).

claim: Both Imp and Syp homologs are highly expressed in the developing mouse brain and play vital roles in neural development.
source: Imp and Syp are evolutionarily conserved, both homologs are highly expressed in the developing mouse brain and play vital roles in neural development, suggesting a fundamental conservation of their function in the development of central nervous (Chen et al., 2012; Mori et al., 2001; Williams et al., 2016).

claim: Imp1 is highly expressed in young neuronal progenitors in mice.
source: For example, Imp1, one of the three mouse orthologs of Imp family, is highly expressed in young neuronal progenitors.

claim: Imp1 promotes the self-renewal state of neuronal stem cells while inhibiting differentiation genes in mice.
source: In particular Imp promotes the self-renewal state of neuronal stem cells while inhibiting differentiation genes (Nishino et al., 2013).

claim: Dysregulation of RNA-binding protein expression is a common feature of neurodegenerative diseases.
source: For example dysregulation of the RBPs expression are a common feature of neurodegenerative diseases (Lenzken et al., 2014).

claim: The Imp family plays a key role in the stem cell physiology of many organs.
source: Interestingly, the Imp family also plays a key role in the stem cell physiology of many other organs and several studies have revealed that the Imp family maintain the proliferative state of different type of cancers (Degrauwe et al., 2016; Bell et al., 2013; Genovese et al., 2019; Lan et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2021).

claim: The Imp family maintains the proliferative state of different types of cancers.
source: Interestingly, the Imp family also plays a key role in the stem cell physiology of many other organs and several studies have revealed that the Imp family maintain the proliferative state of different type of cancers (Degrauwe et al., 2016; Bell et al., 2013; Genovese et al., 2019; Lan et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2021).

claim: Alterations in adult neurogenesis in humans can contribute to psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia.
source: Notably, alterations in adult neurogenesis in humans can contribute to psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia (Allen et al., 2016; Mahar et al., 2014) and autism (Hazlett et al., 2017; Wegiel et al., 2010) or neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer (Gallardo, 2019).

claim: Alterations in adult neurogenesis in humans can contribute to autism.
source: Notably, alterations in adult neurogenesis in humans can contribute to psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia (Allen et al., 2016; Mahar et al., 2014) and autism (Hazlett et al., 2017; Wegiel et al., 2010) or neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer (Gallardo, 2019).

claim: Alterations in adult neurogenesis in humans can contribute to neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer.
source: Notably, alterations in adult neurogenesis in humans can contribute to psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia (Allen et al., 2016; Mahar et al., 2014) and autism (Hazlett et al., 2017; Wegiel et al., 2010) or neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer (Gallardo, 2019).

claim: Disruptions in neurodevelopmental programs are often observed in brain tumors.
source: Disruptions in neurodevelopmental programs are often observed in brain tumors, and tumors that arise in early childhood may be attributed to a dysregulation in the molecular machinery governing the termination of neurogenesis (Jessa et al., 2019).

claim: Tumors that arise in early childhood may be attributed to a dysregulation in the molecular machinery governing the termination of neurogenesis.
source: Disruptions in neurodevelopmental programs are often observed in brain tumors, and tumors that arise in early childhood may be attributed to a dysregulation in the molecular machinery governing the termination of neurogenesis (Jessa et al., 2019).

claim: Variations in the number of neurons contribute to changes in neuronal circuits and behaviors in insects.
source: Recent studies in insects have indicated that variations in the number of neurons contribute to changes in neuronal circuits and behaviors (Pop et al., 2020; Prieto-Godino et al., 2020).

claim: In Drosophila, adult neurons and glia are mostly produced during larval and pupal stages by stem cells called neuroblasts.
source: In Drosophila, adult neurons and glia are mostly produced during larval and pupal stages by stem cells called neuroblast (NB).

claim: Neuroblasts undergo asymmetric divisions to self-renew and generate neuronal and glial progenies either directly or indirectly.
source: Similar to vertebrates, NBs undergo asymmetric divisions to self-renew and generate neuronal and glial progenies either directly or indirectly.

claim: Type I neuroblasts generate ganglion mother cells that divide once to produce neurons and glia.
source: Type I NBs generate ganglion mother cells (GMCs) that divide once to produce neurons and glia (Doe et al., 1985; Karcavich and Doe, 2005) while type II NBs generate intermediate neuronal progenitors that undergo multiple divisions to generate glia and/or neurons (Homem et al., 2015; Bello et al., 2008; Bowman et al., 2008).

claim: Type II neuroblasts generate intermediate neuronal progenitors that undergo multiple divisions to generate glia and/or neurons.
source: Type I NBs generate ganglion mother cells (GMCs) that divide once to produce neurons and glia (Doe et al., 1985; Karcavich and Doe, 2005) while type II NBs generate intermediate neuronal progenitors that undergo multiple divisions to generate glia and/or neurons (Homem et al., 2015; Bello et al., 2008; Bowman et al., 2008).

claim: Under normal conditions, each neuroblast in Drosophila produces a consistent number of mature neurons.
source: Under normal conditions, each NB in Drosophila produces a consistent number of mature neurons, although this number can vary between different NBs.

claim: The precise generation of a stereotypical number of progenies depends on three key parameters: the speed of neuroblast division, the timing of neuroblast neurogenesis termination, and programmed cell death during the asymmetric division of ganglion mother cells.
source: The precise generation of a stereotypical number of progenies depends on three key parameters: the speed of NB division, the timing of NB neurogenesis termination, and programmed cell death (PCD) during the asymmetric division of GMCs.

claim: Most type I and II neuroblasts end neurogenesis during the early pupal stages either by accumulating the transcription factor Prospero or through a combination of autophagy and programmed cell death.
source: Most type I and II NBs end neurogenesis during the early pupal stages either by accumulating the transcription factor (TF) Prospero, triggering symmetrical division and resulting in two postmitotic cells (Homem et al., 2014; Maurange et al., 2008) or through a combination of autophagy and PCD (Pahl et al., 2019; Siegrist et al., 2010).

claim: All neuroblasts experience a decrease in size prior to the termination of neurogenesis.
source: Prior to the termination of neurogenesis, all NBs experience a decrease in size (Homem et al., 2014; Maurange et al., 2008).

claim: The reduction in size of neuroblasts ending neurogenesis early in pupal stages is linked to a metabolic switch that enhances oxidative phosphorylation.
source: The reduction in size of NBs ending neurogenesis early in pupal stages is linked to a metabolic switch that enhances oxidative phosphorylation, leading to a terminal differentiation division (Homem et al., 2014).

claim: The decrease in size observed in neuroblasts terminating neurogenesis later correlates with a reduction in the activity of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase.
source: Conversely, the decrease in size observed in NBs terminating neurogenesis later, such as mushroom body NBs, correlates with a reduction in the activity of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase, which acts as an autophagy inhibitor (Homem et al., 2014; Pahl et al., 2019).

claim: The temporal control of neuroblast decommissioning is influenced by extrinsic signals like the steroid hormone ecdysone.
source: The temporal control of decommissioning is influenced by extrinsic signals like the steroid hormone ecdysone (Homem et al., 2014; Pahl et al., 2019) and as well as an intrinsic program characterized by the sequential expression of temporal RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) such as Imp (insulin-like growth factor 2 (IGF2) messenger RNA (mRNA)-binding proteins) and Syp (Syncrip) expressed in opposite temporal gradients within the NB, or through a temporal cascade of TFs.

claim: Mushroom body neuroblasts decommission during the late pupal stage due to a prolonged expression of Imp compared to other neuroblasts.
source: For instance, mushroom body NBs decommission during the late pupal stage due to a prolonged expression of Imp compared to other NBs (Yang et al., 2017).

claim: In the ventral nerve cord, the timing of neuroblast decommissioning is determined by temporal transcription factors, leading to apoptosis in type II neuroblasts or terminal division in type I neuroblasts.
source: In the ventral nerve cord (VNC, analogous to our spinal cord), the timing of NB decommissioning is determined by temporal TFs, leading to apoptosis in type II NBs or terminal division in type 1 NBs (Maurange et al., 2008).

claim: The decommissioning of neuroblasts is spatially regulated by spatial selectors such as Hox genes.
source: Lastly, the decommissioning of NBs is also spatially regulated by spatial selectors such as Hox genes. For example, NB5-6 in thoracic segments produces a greater number of neurons compared to NB5-6 in the abdomen, due to the absence of abdominal Hox genes (Karlsson et al., 2010).

claim: On average, neuroblast divisions in larvae occur at a speed of approximately 80-90 min per division.
source: On average, NB divisions in larvae occur at a speed of approximately 80–90 min per division. However, this speed varies among different NBs (Hailstone et al., 2020).

claim: The heterogeneity in neuroblast division speed appears to be regulated by the opposing temporal gradients of Imp and Syp within the neuroblast.
source: The heterogeneity in NB division speed appears to be regulated by the opposing temporal gradients of Imp and Syp within the NB. Imp promotes high-speed division by stabilizing myc RNA and increasing Myc protein levels, while Syp has an inhibitory effect on NB division speed by directly inhibiting Imp as development progresses (Samuels et al., 2020).

claim: Imp promotes high-speed division by stabilizing myc RNA and increasing Myc protein levels.
source: Imp promotes high-speed division by stabilizing myc RNA and increasing Myc protein levels, while Syp has an inhibitory effect on NB division speed by directly inhibiting Imp as development progresses (Samuels et al., 2020).

claim: Syp has an inhibitory effect on neuroblast division speed by directly inhibiting Imp as development progresses.
source: Imp promotes high-speed division by stabilizing myc RNA and increasing Myc protein levels, while Syp has an inhibitory effect on NB division speed by directly inhibiting Imp as development progresses (Samuels et al., 2020).

claim: Between 40% and 50% of hemi-lineages derived from type I neuroblasts undergo programmed cell death.
source: Between 40% and 50% of hemi-lineages derived from type I NBs undergo PCD (Kumar et al., 2009; Truman et al., 2010).

claim: When programmed cell death is blocked in the midline neuroblasts of the ventral nerve cord, the 'undead' neurons differentiate and form complex and functional arborizations.
source: Interestingly, when PCD is blocked in the midline NBs of the VNC, the 'undead' neurons differentiate and form complex and functional arborizations (Pop et al., 2020).

claim: Variation in programmed cell death patterns between different insect species could change their behavior.
source: Recent studies have demonstrated how variation in PCD patterns between different insect species could change their behavior suggesting that probably all mechanisms controlling the number of neurons potentially play a role during the behavior evolution (Pop et al., 2020; Prieto-Godino et al., 2020).

claim: Lin A/15 neuroblast dedicates 40% of its time to producing immature motoneurons that are subsequently eliminated through apoptosis.
source: Intriguingly, Lin A/15 NB dedicates 40% of its time to producing immature MNs (iMNs) that are subsequently eliminated through apoptosis.

claim: Imp+ motoneurons survive, while Imp-, Syp+ motoneurons undergo apoptosis.
source: Imp+ MNs survive, while Imp−, Syp+ MNs undergo apoptosis.

claim: Imp promotes survival in immature motoneurons.
source: Genetic experiments show that Imp promotes survival, whereas Syp promotes cell death in iMNs.

claim: Syp promotes cell death in immature motoneurons.
source: Genetic experiments show that Imp promotes survival, whereas Syp promotes cell death in iMNs.

claim: Late-born motoneurons fail to express a functional code of transcription factors that control their morphological fate and are subject to elimination.
source: Late-born MNs, which fail to express a functional code of transcription factors (mTFs) that control their morphological fate, are subject to elimination.

claim: Manipulating the expression of Imp and Syp in Lin A/15 neuroblast and progeny leads to a shift of transcription factor code in late-born motoneurons toward that of early-born motoneurons, and their survival.
source: Manipulating the expression of Imp and Syp in Lin A/15 NB and progeny leads to a shift of TF code in late-born MNs toward that of early-born MNs, and their survival.

claim: Introducing the transcription factor code of early-born motoneurons into late-born motoneurons promotes their survival.
source: Additionally, introducing the TF code of early-born MNs into late-born MNs also promoted their survival.

claim: The differential expression of Imp and Syp in immature motoneurons links precise neuronal generation and distinct identities through the regulation of morphological transcription factors.
source: These findings demonstrate that the differential expression of Imp and Syp in iMNs links precise neuronal generation and distinct identities through the regulation of mTFs.

claim: Both Imp and Syp are conserved in vertebrates.
source: Both Imp and Syp are conserved in vertebrates, suggesting that they play a fundamental role in precise neurogenesis across species.
